title: Possessives and reflexive pronouns
intro: Words that show who owns something: my and mine, 's and of, and the reflexive pronouns such as myself.

sources.label: British Council: Capital letters and apostrophes

sections.title: Possessive adjectives and pronouns
sections.summary: A possessive adjective goes before a noun. A possessive pronoun replaces the noun.

tables.caption: Subject, possessive adjective and possessive pronoun
head: subject
adjective (before a noun)
pronoun (alone)
example
rows: This is my bag. The bag is mine.
Is that your phone? Is it yours?
His car is red. The red car is his.
Her sister is a doctor. The doctor is hers.
Our house is small. The small house is ours.
Their dog is friendly. The dog is theirs.

uses: Use a possessive adjective before a noun: my book, your idea.
Use a possessive pronoun when the noun is already clear: Whose pen is this? It is mine.
The word depends on the owner, not on the thing: Mary loves her dog (a woman owns it), John loves his dog.
Use the adjective with parts of the body and clothes: I washed my hands. He put on his coat.
A friend of mine, a cousin of hers: of + possessive pronoun.

examples.text: Is this your umbrella or mine?
The children left their bags in the hall.
Its is for things and animals. It's means it is or it has.
examples.note: Do not mix up its and it's.

mistakes.why: Do not use the adjective without a noun. Use the pronoun.
Its (no apostrophe) shows possession. It's means it is.

mistakes.wrong: She is a friend of her.
mistakes.right: She is a friend of hers.
mistakes.why: After of use the possessive pronoun.

checks.question: Complete: These keys are not ___ (I). Are they yours?
checks.explanation: A pronoun stands alone after be.

checks.question: Choose: The company changed (it's / its) logo.
checks.explanation: Possession needs its without an apostrophe.

sections.title: Possessive 's and of
sections.summary: Use 's for the possessions of people and animals. Use of for things.
uses: Use 's for people, animals and groups: the teacher's desk, the dog's bowl, the team's coach.
Use of for things: the end of the film, the top of the page.
Time and place words often take 's: today's news, yesterday's match, a week's holiday.
You can leave out the noun when it is clear: We went to Sam's (house). She is at the dentist's.
James's or James' are both correct. Say the extra s.

examples.text: The girls' changing room is on the left.
What is the name of the hotel?
Whose bike is this? It is Ben's.

mistakes.why: Children is plural without -s, so add 's.
Use 's for a person, not of.
Do not use the with a possessive 's.

checks.question: Complete: This is the room of my sister. (Use 's)
checks.explanation: Use 's for a person. Do not add the.

sections.title: Reflexive pronouns
sections.summary: Use a reflexive pronoun when the subject and the object are the same person, or for emphasis.
uses: The subject does the action to itself: He hurt himself. I looked at myself.
For emphasis: I made the cake myself (nobody helped).
With by: by myself means alone. She lives by herself.
Use each other for an action between two or more people: They looked at each other.
Do not use a reflexive after verbs such as wash, shave, dress and relax when the meaning is clear: I got up and dressed.

examples.text: Did you enjoy yourself at the party?
They help each other with homework.
examples.note: Each other = A helps B and B helps A.

mistakes.why: Do not use a reflexive after feel when the meaning is simple.

mistakes.wrong: We looked at ourselves in the photo. (meaning: one at the other)
mistakes.why: Use each other for a two-way action.

checks.question: Complete: The two friends smiled at ___ .
